title: Whom shall I fear? (Psalm 27)
hook: the Lord is my light; one thing I ask, to dwell in his house

segments.voice: Yesterday, Psalm twenty-two: My God, my God, a cry that still says my God, and turns to praise. Your line was even he cried this. Did you sit with someone in a hard first line? Day four hundred seventeen.

One request. Not three wishes. Not a list. One. It's harder than it sounds. Health. Safety for the people we love. A little more money. The scan coming back clear. The person who left coming back. Psalm twenty-seven is sung by someone surrounded: enemies closing in, an army camped around, false witnesses lining up, and he even imagines his own father and mother turning away. If anyone has a long list of requests, it's him. And then he says: I've asked for one thing. Only one.
screen: `IF YOU COULD ASK FOR ONE THING.` → `SURROUNDED, WITH A LONG LIST.` → `ONLY ONE.`

segments.voice: Psalm twenty-seven opens, in the King James Bible: "The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?" Two questions, and they're not quite rhetorical. The psalmist knows exactly whom he could fear. He names them: evildoers, a host encamped against him, war rising up. The fear is real. The questions are his way of standing up inside it. Then, the one thing: "One thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life, to behold the beauty of the LORD, and to enquire in his temple." Not rescue first. Not victory. Nearness. To live close to God, and to look at his beauty. Everything else, the psalm seems to say, follows from that one thing, or matters less without it. The psalm doesn't pretend the fear goes away all at once. Halfway through it swings back to pleading: hide not thy face from me. Then a tender line: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up." And it ends not with a victory but with waiting: "Wait on the LORD: be of good courage, and he shall strengthen thine heart: wait, I say, on the LORD." Twice. Wait. Two things worth knowing. Jewish custom adds Psalm twenty-seven to daily prayer in the weeks around the High Holy Days in the fall. And the first words, in Latin, Dominus illuminatio mea, the Lord is my light, are the motto of the University of Oxford.
screen: `TWO QUESTIONS, ASKED INSIDE FEAR.` · `ONE THING: TO DWELL NEAR.` · `WHEN MY FATHER AND MOTHER FORSAKE ME.` · `WAIT, AND BE OF GOOD COURAGE.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS MY LIGHT; WHOM SHALL I FEAR?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the one thing you'd ask. Settle, and breathe. Let your list of wants come up: all of it, the big and the small. Don't fight it. Then begin setting things down, one by one, like taking items out of an overfull bag. Keep going until you're holding one thing. Just one. It may surprise you. It may be close to the psalmist's, or something else entirely. Hold it. If you pray, you can ask God for it plainly. If you don't, just let yourself know what it is. The bell holds the time.
False witnesses. People lining up against the psalmist, one of the real dangers he names before asking for just one thing.
Your line: one thing I ask. Today, when you catch yourself wanting ten things at once, come back to your one. Day four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Some Christians pray Psalm 27 in times of fear, and it appears in daily prayer; in Jewish practice it is recited daily from the start of the month of Elul through the autumn festivals.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brave psalm about not being scared.
what it means: courage asked from inside real fear, and one request above all: to be near God.
what a scholar hears: Dominus illuminatio mea (Vulgate Psalm 26), Oxford's motto; and the psalm's place in Jewish prayer through Elul and the High Holy Days.

notes: Editor review (y2 days 407–424): hook rewritten (dropped "Most of us would struggle" and the banned "Now picture"); "the most tender line" softened; "A few things worth knowing" made "Two things"; Jewish custom stated as custom and Oxford's motto no longer "for centuries"; howItsDone "often" removed.
27:10 is conditional ('When my father and my mother forsake me'); the hook says he imagines it. Confirm.
Jewish custom: Psalm 27 recited from Rosh Chodesh Elul through Hoshana Rabbah (or Shemini Atzeret); the script says 'for weeks around the High Holy Days in the fall'. Confirm.
Oxford motto 'Dominus illuminatio mea' (Psalm 26:1 in the Vulgate numbering); confirm.
Original: אַחַת שָׁאַלְתִּי; KJV renders 'One thing have I desired'. Confirm the gloss 'asked'.
